message.content: {"executive_summary":"This simulation modeled the evacuation of 150 agents initially concentrated in Room 1, funneling through a 1.2 m doorway into a corridor, then into Room 2 and out an exit. The narrow door was intended as the primary flow‐limiting bottleneck to induce upstream congestion. However, the run output lacked any time‐series or spatial occupancy data—no evacuated counts per step, zone occupancies, density measures, or agent trajectories—so quantitative characterization of evacuation phases, flow rates, or emergent queuing patterns is not possible.","conclusions":["150 agents began in Room 1 and all must pass through a single 1.2 m bottleneck door to exit.","The model’s spatial layout (Room 1 → door → corridor → Room 2 → exit) is appropriate for generating bottleneck effects, but no empirical flow data were recorded.","Absence of per‐step evacuated_count and zone‐based occupancy time series prevents measurement of evacuation rate, phase transitions, or tipping points.","Without spatial or interaction metrics, clustering, queue formation, and corridor congestion remain unverified and any emergent behaviors (e.g. oscillations or lane formation) cannot be substantiated.","The current output supports only structural and configurational verification, not dynamic outcome analysis."],"recommendations":["Instrument the model to record per‐step evacuated_count and occupancy counts for each zone to quantify evacuation dynamics.","Log agent positions or aggregate density heatmaps at regular intervals to characterize spatial congestion and queue formation.","Compute and export flow‐rate metrics through the 1.2 m door (agents per time step) to identify bottleneck capacity and phase transitions.","Perform parameter sweeps on door width and corridor length to evaluate sensitivity of congestion and evacuation time to geometry.","Run multiple replicates and aggregate results to reduce stochastic variability and enable statistical analysis of emergent behaviors."]}
